Here is a comprehensive summary of the safety actions taken regarding **loperamide (Imodium)** — including a market withdrawal of a specific formulation, a Black Box Warning, and multiple FDA Drug Safety Communications:

---

## 🔴 1. Market Withdrawal: Loperamide Infant/Children's Drops and Syrup (1990)


In the 1980s, loperamide existed in the form of drops (Imodium Drops), initially intended for children's usage. Johnson & Johnson **voluntarily withdrew it from the market in 1990** after 18 cases of paralytic ileus (resulting in six deaths) were registered in Pakistan and reported by the World Health Organization (WHO).



The leading international supplier, Johnson and Johnson, informed WHO that having regard to the dangers inherent in improper use and overdosing, this formulation (Imodium Drops) was voluntarily withdrawn from Pakistan in March 1990. The company subsequently decided not only to withdraw this preparation worldwide, but also to remove all syrup formulations from countries where WHO had a programme for the control of diarrhoeal diseases.



In the following years (1990–1991), products containing loperamide were restricted for children's use in several countries (ranging from two to five years of age).


📌 **Source:** Wikipedia – Loperamide: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loperamide

---

## 🔴 2. FDA Black Box Warning (2016)


The FDA undertook stringent measures after the 2014–2016 increase in deaths due to cardiac causes secondary to loperamide abuse. **In June 2016, the FDA issued a Black Box Warning** about serious heart problems, including Torsades de Pointes, cardiac arrest, and sudden cardiac death with high doses of loperamide use. In April 2017, the FDA ordered an additional alert along with the Black Box Warning.



In June 2016, the FDA released a Drug Safety Communication stating that loperamide was causing serious and fatal cardiac events (e.g., QT-interval prolongation, TdP, syncope, and cardiac arrest). Additionally, the FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research approved a safety-related drug labeling change in November 2016. A black box warning was added to Imodium's package insert stating that "Cases of Torsades de Pointes, cardiac arrest, and death have been reported with the use of a higher than recommended dosages of IMODIUM."



Loperamide **has a boxed warning** for torsades de pointes and sudden death when used in higher-than-recommended doses.


📌 **Sources:**
- NIH/StatPearls – Loperamide: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557885/
- PMC – Rising Concern of Loperamide Abuse: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6944144/
- FDA Label (NDC 67296-0129): https://ndclist.com/ndc/67296-0129/label

---

## 🔴 3. FDA Drug Safety Communications (2016 & 2018)


The FDA's package insert for Imodium carries the Black Box Warning: "Cases of Torsades de Pointes, cardiac arrest, and death have been reported with the use of higher than recommended dosages of IMODIUM." In **2016 and 2018**, the FDA released two Drug Safety Communications on loperamide, which warned about the serious heart risks of extreme doses and asked for packaging changes to encourage safe use.



The FDA warned that taking higher than recommended doses of loperamide (Imodium), including through abuse or misuse of the product, **can cause serious life-threatening arrhythmias that can lead to death**. The risk of these serious life-threatening arrhythmias may also be increased when high doses of loperamide are taken with several kinds of medicines that interact with loperamide.


📌 **Source:** ACCP – FDA Warning RE Loperamide: https://accp1.org/Members/ACCP1/5Publications_and_News/FDA_Warning_RE_Loperamide.aspx

---

## 🔴 4. Packaging Restrictions (2018–2019)


In January 2018, the FDA started working with manufacturers to use blister packs or other single-dose packaging and to limit the number of doses per package of loperamide that could be sold OTC. More recently, in September 2019, the FDA approved the new packaging for the brand name OTC loperamide in an attempt to prevent abuse and misuse.



The maximum allowed daily dose of OTC loperamide for adult usage is 8 mg/day. The new carton is to contain no more than 48 mg of loperamide and requires unit-dose blister packaging.


📌 **Source:** FDA Communication (January 30, 2018): https://www.fda.gov/files/FDA-limits-packaging-for-anti-diarrhea-medicine-loperamide-(Imodium)-to-encourage-safe-use_PDF.pdf

---

## 🟡 5. Early Schedule V Classification (Later Removed)


When loperamide was introduced in 1977, the FDA initially placed it in the Schedule V list of controlled medications, basing their decision on animal data that suggested loperamide had produced opioid-like effects. Loperamide was later **removed from the Schedule V list** and became a nonprescription product by 1988 due to several volunteer studies and epidemiological data that demonstrated a low risk of physical dependence and abuse.


📌 **Source:** PowerPak CE – Pharmacist Review of Loperamide Abuse: https://journalce.powerpak.com/ce/pharmacist-review-of-loperamide-abuse

---

## Summary Table

| Action | Year | Details |
|---|---|---|
| WHO/J&J Withdrawal of Infant Drops & Syrup | 1990 | Voluntary global withdrawal due to 18 paralytic ileus cases (6 deaths) in Pakistan |
| Schedule V Classification (then removed) | 1977–1988 | Initially classified as controlled; later removed from Schedule V |
| FDA Black Box Warning Added | 2016 | For Torsades de Pointes, cardiac arrest, and death at high doses |
| FDA Drug Safety Communications | 2016 & 2018 | Warned about fatal cardiac risks; requested labeling and packaging changes |
| OTC Packaging Restrictions | 2018–2019 | Required blister packs; limited pack size to max 48 mg (24 count) |

**Bottom line:** Loperamide has **not been fully withdrawn from the market globally** as an adult drug, but a specific pediatric formulation (infant drops/syrup) was voluntarily withdrawn worldwide in 1990. It **does carry a current Black Box Warning** in the United States related to fatal cardiac arrhythmias from high-dose use or abuse.

Here is a comprehensive, cited summary of the regulatory safety actions taken globally regarding **Montelukast (brand name: Singulair)**:

---

## ⚠️ Montelukast (Singulair): Black Box Warnings & Safety Actions

### Has Montelukast Been Withdrawn from the Market?

**No.** Montelukast has **not** been withdrawn from any major market or discontinued for safety reasons. It remains available by prescription globally. However, it has attracted significant and escalating safety warnings across multiple countries due to serious neuropsychiatric side effects.

---

### 🇺🇸 United States (FDA) — Black Box Warning (2020)


On **March 4, 2020**, the FDA strengthened existing warnings about serious behavior and mood-related changes with montelukast (brand name Singulair), a prescription medicine for asthma and allergy.



The FDA added a **black box warning** to montelukast in 2020 due to reports of serious neuropsychiatric events, including agitation, depression, suicidal thoughts, and behavior. This decision was based on accumulating evidence from post-marketing surveillance and clinical studies, indicating that these adverse effects, although rare, were significant enough to warrant the highest level of caution.



The FDA decided a stronger warning was needed after conducting an extensive review of available information and convening a panel of outside experts. They required a **Boxed Warning** — their most prominent warning — to be added to the prescribing information, as well as a new patient Medication Guide.



Of the over 19,000 reports of adverse events that the FDA received since the drug's approval in 1998, more than 10,000 were about psychiatric or nervous system adverse events. These included aggression, irritability, agitation, disorientation, hallucinations, insomnia, memory impairment, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, anxiety, depression, suicidal thoughts, and even suicide. More than 7,000 of those adverse events are considered serious, and from 1998 to 2019, FDA received reports of 82 suicides among people using Singulair.



Given the available information, the FDA also reevaluated the benefits and risks of montelukast and determined it should **not be the first-choice treatment for mild allergic rhinitis**.



Data from the FDA's Sentinel System (collected between 2010 and 2015) did not show an increased risk of neuropsychiatric events in approximately 450,000 asthmatics older than age 6 taking montelukast vs. inhaled corticosteroids, and other observational studies also did not find an increased risk of mental health side effects. That being said, the reports of suicide along with evidence that montelukast crosses the blood-brain barrier in animal models persuaded the FDA to strengthen their warning.


**Source:** [FDA Drug Safety Communication — FDA.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-boxed-warning-about-serious-mental-health-side-effects-asthma-and-allergy-drug)

---

### 🇬🇧 United Kingdom (MHRA) — Strengthened Warnings (2019 & 2024)


In a statement published on **April 29, 2024**, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) said that "more prominent warnings" would be added to the patient information leaflet (PIL) provided with every pack of montelukast in the UK. The warnings in the PIL and summary of product characteristics for all montelukast products were strengthened and highlighted with a **black box** for greater emphasis.



In **March 2024**, the MHRA announced a safety review of montelukast following an increased number of Yellow Card reports from patients who experienced suspected neuropsychiatric adverse reactions, including suicidal behaviour. Since montelukast was first authorised in the UK in 1998, approximately 44 million prescriptions have been issued, during which time there have been 1,223 reports of suspected neuropsychiatric adverse reactions.


**Source:** [The Pharmaceutical Journal](https://pharmaceutical-journal.com/article/news/montelukast-will-carry-more-prominent-warnings-of-neuropsychiatric-reactions) | [MHRA Drug Safety Update — GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/montelukast-singulair-reminder-of-the-risk-of-neuropsychiatric-reactions)

---

### 🇪🇺 European Union (EMA/PRAC) — Strengthened Warnings (2019–2023)


In **2019**, the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) recommended an update of the product information of medicines containing montelukast to include strengthened warnings about neuropsychiatric events. A decentralised procedure to implement the PRAC recommendations was finalised in **April 2023**, with the warning in the product information highlighted in **bold type font within a black box**.


**Source:** [European Parliament — Answer for Question E-002177/23](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-9-2023-002177-ASW_EN.html)

---

### 🇦🇺 Australia (TGA) — Updated Safety Warnings (2024–2025)


Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) conducted a safety investigation in **2024** after international regulators strengthened warnings about neuropsychiatric events for montelukast products. The update brought the Australian Product Information (PI) and Consumer Medicine Information (CMI) in line with international regulatory advice.



In rare cases, patients taking montelukast have died after experiencing suicidal behaviour. Health professionals should be vigilant for neuropsychiatric reactions in patients taking montelukast and discontinue treatment if new or worsening symptoms occur.



An expert group recommended adding a **boxed warning** in the Australian product information to align with international regulators. A search of Australia's publicly available Database of Adverse Event Notifications identified 356 cases for montelukast and psychiatric disorders, with the most commonly reported symptoms being aggression (100 cases), anxiety (87 cases), suicidal ideation (72 cases), and depression (71 cases).


**Source:** [TGA Safety Update — TGA.gov.au](https://www.tga.gov.au/news/safety-updates/more-prominent-safety-warnings-about-neuropsychiatric-effects-montelukast)

---

### Neuropsychiatric Effects After Discontinuation


The FDA's boxed warning also includes the statement that "most reported cases of neuropsychiatric events occurred during montelukast treatment, but some occurred after discontinuation" and that "in some cases symptoms persisted after stopping montelukast or were reported after discontinuation of therapy."


---

### Summary Table

| Regulatory Body | Country | Action | Year |
|---|---|---|---|
| FDA | USA | **Black Box Warning** issued; restricted use for mild allergic rhinitis | 2020 |
| MHRA | UK | Reminder (2019), then strengthened **black box** warning | 2019, 2024 |
| EMA/PRAC | EU | Strengthened warning (black box in product info) | 2019–2023 |
| TGA | Australia | Strengthened warning (black box added) | 2024 |

**Bottom line:** Montelukast has **never been withdrawn from the market** for safety reasons. However, it has received **black box warnings** (the highest level of drug safety warning) in the US
